channel.title: Daily Digest
channel.description: Curated tech blog summaries, inspired by Andrej Karpathy's reading list

item.title: “It Gives Great Demo”
item.description: The article explores the concept of 'it gives great demo,' highlighting how some products or individuals excel at initial presentation while failing in long-term practical utility. It argues that while flashy features capture attention, truly great products eventually become invisible through seamless integration.

item.title: This Week in Source Control: 4 November 2026
item.description: This post provides a weekly digest of developments in version control, specifically focusing on OpenAI's implementation of Pando to scale their Git monorepo. It also compares design approaches for massive repositories, contrasting OpenAI's infrastructure with discussions surrounding Anthropic's Scion and Databricks' Mononoke.

item.title: There are things with ranks, but it’s not always clear what the ranks mean
item.description: This post highlights the common pitfall in technical documentation where experts assume too much prior knowledge from the reader. It emphasizes the need for clarity and context when explaining features that involve ranking systems.

item.title: Book Review: Practice by Rosalind Brown ★★★★☆
item.description: Terence Eden reviews Rosalind Brown's book 'Practice', a day-in-the-life narrative that he describes as a stunning and Proustian experience. He maintains a personal policy of purchasing books written by people he meets, which has led him to discover this delightful work.

item.title: Pluralistic: The AI fatfinger economy has come for my receipts app (04 Nov 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques the current trend of tech companies forcing AI features into user interfaces, labeling it the 'AI fatfinger economy.' He argues this UI manipulation is a continuation of past corporate tactics used to inflate valuation for investors at the expense of user experience.

item.title: Goodhart's Law, but We Already Spent All Our Money
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: The article critiques how modern industries, including sports, video games, and AI, are exclusively valued by their monetary output rather than their inherent quality or community impact. It applies Goodhart's Law to explain that using financial metrics as targets leads to distorted outcomes, such as the current trend of over-investing in AI to project success.

item.title: datasette-llm 0.1a10
item.description: Simon Willison has released version 0.1a10 of datasette-llm. This update specifically fixes a bug that incorrectly handled model restriction settings on the agent.datasette.io demo site.

item.title: datasette-apps 0.3a0
item.description: Datasette Apps 0.3a0 introduces enhanced integration with Datasette Agent, allowing users to create and manage custom HTML applications directly via chat. The update features improved autocomplete for app references and new tools for managing stored queries with mandatory user approval for write operations.

item.title: datasette-agent 0.5a0
item.description: Datasette Agent 0.5a0 introduces a new 'panel' feature that allows users to chat with an AI agent alongside their data-driven applications. This release enables users to build and modify database-backed apps directly through a split-screen interface.

item.title: llm 0.37.1
item.description: Simon Willison has released version 0.37.1 of the LLM command-line utility. This update serves as a bugfix release and includes contributions from several community developers.

item.title: New Article, Annual LFP Charity Discount
item.description: The author announced a new article discussing the trade-offs between Deterministic Simulation Testing and Formal Methods. Additionally, they are hosting a charity drive for the Greater Chicago Food Depository, offering their 'Logic for Programmers' book at a 50% discount until the end of the month.

item.title: Runs scored in World Baseball Classic
item.description: The author shares their methodology for accurately predicting the total number of runs in the 2026 World Baseball Classic knockout stage. By comparing a simple baseline guess with granular count modeling techniques, the article illustrates a statistical approach to sports forecasting.

item.title: Pumpkin Seeds
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: This post explores the cultural fascination with Halloween, focusing on the enduring popularity of cryptids like the Mothman. It reflects on how monsters remain a staple of seasonal pop culture through various media and storytelling traditions.

item.title: I wish tech companies knew more about me
item.description: The author challenges the narrative that tech companies have omniscient knowledge of their users, providing personal anecdotes where algorithms fail to deliver relevant ads or recognize simple behavioral patterns. These experiences highlight significant flaws in current data collection and personalization efforts, suggesting that big data remains surprisingly ineffective.

item.title: Fraction comparison trick revisited
item.description: This article examines a mathematical curiosity regarding fraction comparisons, where the inequality a/b > c/d is often implied by the condition a + d > b + c. The author discusses the rigorous probabilistic proof for this phenomenon by evaluating the limit as the range of chosen integers approaches infinity.

item.title: Euclidean, Spherical, and Projective Geometry
item.description: This article explores the relationships between Euclidean, spherical, and projective geometries by revisiting the foundational postulates of Euclid. It highlights how these distinct geometric systems are interconnected despite their perceived differences in tangibility and complexity.

item.title: How a programming might reinvent the projective plane
item.description: This post explores how practical programming techniques used by graphics developers can lead to a rigorous mathematical definition of the projective plane. It discusses the process of adding 'points at infinity' to the Euclidean plane to resolve geometric intersections.

item.title: How do you implement a random-access database when you don’t have random-access external storage?
item.description: This post provides a concise solution for implementing a random-access database in environments lacking random-access external storage. The author suggests storing the entire database directly in the application's memory.

item.title: Just a little AI resistance, as a treat
item.description: The author advocates for active public pushback against poor or unethical implementations of AI, exemplified by the 'AI Resist List'. The post highlights the importance of holding organizations accountable for negative AI-driven practices through direct engagement and feedback.

item.title: Pluralistic: Separable (03 Nov 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow reflects on the historical 'Edison Tone Tests' to illustrate how AI decouples creative outputs from their human origins. He argues that our brains are conditioned to assume a performer exists behind every performance, a bias now being exploited by generative technology.

item.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
item.description: The article discusses 'Weight-Space Programming,' a new capability where LLMs can interpret and directly modify the raw numerical weights of other neural networks. The author demonstrates that even local models like Qwen 27B can perform these tasks, effectively improving performance without traditional gradient-based training.

item.title: I discovered a sound that leaks your exact location (and it's everywhere) - YouTube
item.description: This article highlights an innovative OSINT technique that uses ambient airplane engine noise in video recordings to pinpoint a precise location. By analyzing Doppler frequency shifts and cross-referencing them with ADS-B flight data, investigators can track flight paths to geolocate video sources.

item.title: October sponsors-only newsletter
item.description: Simon Willison announces his October newsletter for GitHub sponsors, covering topics such as game development trends, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and LLM updates. The post serves as a gateway for existing and new sponsors to access private content while providing a preview of the previous month's issue.

item.title: Pray for Chaos
item.description: The article contrasts a dangerous, centralized 'order' in AI development with a chaotic, decentralized future. It argues that if AI cannot be perfectly secured, society will likely move toward fragmentation and vulnerability, potentially leading to the realization of the 'dead Internet' theory.

item.title: Making peace with the projective plane
item.description: The article discusses the realization that projective space and homogeneous coordinates are natural concepts rather than arbitrary abstractions. It emphasizes the importance of providing mathematical motivation when teaching abstract topics to students.

item.title: Sneaking into the auditorium for the Windows 2000 launch rehearsal
item.description: This post recounts a brief personal anecdote about a case of mistaken identity during a rehearsal for the Windows 2000 product launch. It offers a nostalgic, behind-the-scenes glimpse into the historical atmosphere of early Microsoft event planning.

item.title: Lorem Ipsum Dot Gov Dot UK
item.description: The author discusses the perils of testing in production and highlights the importance of using high-quality dummy content. He argues that readable test text is essential to prevent management from misinterpreting placeholder data during the development process.

item.title: Pluralistic: Autodoxing (02 Nov 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques the history of flawed tech policies and the ongoing erosion of digital privacy. He argues that the detrimental consequences of surveillance-friendly legislation, such as the Clipper chip and weakened encryption, were both foreseeable and long warned against by rights advocates.

item.title: Prove you are not a child
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: The author argues against mandatory age verification systems for social media and operating systems, highlighting the severe privacy and security risks associated with sharing sensitive biometric or government data. They contend that these enforcement methods create digital vulnerabilities and punish adults rather than effectively protecting children.

item.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
item.description: Major tech companies, led by Google, have dismantled a massive botnet that compromised over 1.3 million Android TV boxes. This operation effectively cut off the botnet's access to millions of additional IoT devices used for illicit proxy services and ad fraud.

item.title: llm 0.37
item.description: Simon Willison has released version 0.37 of the LLM CLI tool and Python library, featuring new model support, configuration updates, and improved embedding capabilities. He also shares his positive experience using AI-assisted tools to manage and triage a large volume of community-contributed pull requests.

item.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
item.description: Simon Willison revisits the U.S. Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey to update a chart regarding corporate AI adoption rates. The post investigates recent data trends while highlighting how a new Executive Order on 'Super Intelligence' has impacted the Bureau's data reporting and survey structure.

item.title: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing neural network weights
item.description: This article examines the limitations of Large Language Models when it comes to interpreting or manipulating neural network weights. It argues that while LLMs excel at general language tasks, they lack the specialized capability required to perform complex analysis on low-level weight architecture.

item.title: Audience capture
item.description: The article explores the concept of 'audience capture,' a phenomenon where creators unconsciously shift their content to satisfy the preferences of their audience. This cycle can trap creators in a feedback loop that diminishes their original creative intent over time.

item.title: Reliably aligning LLMs is impossible in principle
item.description: This article explores the theoretical limitations of aligning Large Language Models, arguing that perfect alignment is mathematically impossible. It posits that inherent contradictions in human values and technical constraints prevent the creation of a reliably aligned system.

item.title: Weekly Update 528: Reading AI-generated Code & the Economics of Solar
item.description: This update discusses the controversy surrounding Proton's recent engineering manifesto and the public backlash against its CEO's management style. The post critiques the leadership's approach to AI-generated code and organizational communication.

item.title: A Mastodon bot powered by iOS Shortcuts
item.description: The author shares a method for running a Mastodon bot using iOS Shortcuts instead of a traditional server to save on maintenance and costs. By utilizing five interlinked shortcuts, the bot automatically posts quotes from 'The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening' at specific intervals throughout the day.

item.title: A unified view of poles and polars
item.description: This article provides a synthesis of various geometric concepts related to poles and polars, bridging the gap between spherical triangles and projective geometry. It serves as a cohesive overview of the author's previous explorations into these mathematical structures.

item.title: 10 Years on Mastodon
item.description: Terence Eden reflects on his ten-year journey on Mastodon, contrasting the platform's longevity with the rapid decline of many other social networks. The post explores the sustainability of decentralized social media compared to typical short-lived digital services.

item.title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
item.description: When encountering dependency errors while using Python 3.15 with the 'uv' package manager, deleting the 'uv.lock' file often resolves version incompatibility issues. This happens because stale lock files may pin dependencies to versions that do not yet support newer Python releases.

item.title: Quoting Kyle Kingsbury
item.description: Kyle Kingsbury highlights how LLMs undermine trust in software documentation and quality by making it easy to counterfeit signals of maturity. The post poses a critical question for developers on how to maintain and demonstrate software integrity in an era where AI-generated content can obscure authenticity.

item.title: Reading List 10/31/26
item.description: This reading list highlights recent developments in engineering and infrastructure, covering advancements in fiber optic manufacturing and nuclear energy. It also explores critical analysis of transportation safety and aerospace technological progress in China.

item.title: This Week in Package Management: 31 October 2026
item.description: This weekly digest highlights critical security updates for Go, sbt, and pipx, alongside recent releases for Composer and pnpm. Key developments include patching a zip slip vulnerability and new dependency management features for faster and more secure software installation.

item.title: Notes from October 2026
item.description: Evan Hahn summarizes his October 2026 activities, including migrating his website to a CDN-hosted architecture and shipping new automation features at Ghost. The post concludes with a curated list of interesting tech articles covering topics like surveillance, AI, and the nature of software craftsmanship.

item.title: The Microsoft building that was reportedly haunted
item.description: This brief post addresses the long-standing rumors regarding a supposedly haunted Microsoft building. The author notes that despite widespread speculation, there is no credible evidence to support these supernatural claims.

item.title: Gig Review: The Witcher in Concert ★★★★☆
item.description: The author shares their experience attending 'The Witcher in Concert,' a live event featuring an orchestral performance accompanying gameplay footage. They reflect on the rising trend of blending cinema or gaming with live classical music to create immersive experiences.

item.title: Pluralistic: Formalities (31 Oct 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow discusses the US Copyright Office's stance that only human-authored works qualify for copyright, rejecting corporate attempts to claim AI-generated content. He argues that this aligns with the 'sweat of the brow' doctrine, which frames copyright as a reward for human creative effort rather than corporate output.

item.title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
item.description: Parameter Labs discovered a complex exploit in ChatGPT's HTML preview sandbox, allowing unauthorized access to user data. By leveraging a MathLive library vulnerability, attackers could bypass sandbox restrictions to inject malicious HTML and execute scripts via a YouTube oEmbed reflection. This flaw enabled the theft of private user data through crafted ChatGPT share links.

item.title: datasette-llm 0.1a9
item.description: Simon Willison released version 0.1a9 of the datasette-llm plugin, which simplifies the user experience. The update allows the plugin to automatically inherit the default model configured in the LLM tool, removing the need for manual plugin configuration.

item.title: Fast and slow ways to improve your reputation
item.description: This article explores the trade-offs between different strategies for reputation building, contrasting quick wins with long-term approaches. It examines how professional perception is shaped by both immediate actions and sustained consistency.

item.title: Robert Caro – The master biographer reflects at 91
item.description: Renowned biographer Robert Caro reflects on his lifelong dedication to investigative journalism and the extensive archival research behind his works. He expresses a poignant regret regarding the significant amount of discovered information that remains unpublished and unknown to the public.

item.title: Signing and Attestations Across Package Registries
item.description: This article explores the mechanics of package signing and provenance attestations in software registries, contrasting them with traditional Linux distribution build methods. It emphasizes how trusted publishing with OIDC credentials improves security, while noting that attestations are essential for verifying build origins even when credentials are compromised.

item.title: The support case of a customer who said that all they could see was a black screen
item.description: This post recounts a humorous support anecdote where a user reported a 'black screen' issue. The resolution highlights the irony of a customer receiving exactly what they requested, despite their complaints.

item.title: Book Review: The God of Small Things by Arundhati Roy ★★☆☆☆
item.description: The reviewer expresses strong dissatisfaction with Arundhati Roy's 'The God of Small Things,' criticizing the prose as overly melodramatic and exhausting. They describe the narrative as an 'over-sugared mess' that lacks proper pacing and readability.

item.title: College will only cost $20 a month
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: The author reflects on the changing landscape of tech hiring and questions the necessity of expensive traditional university degrees. They propose an alternative model using AI-driven personal tutoring and self-study, weighing the benefits of lower costs against the traditional value of campus networking and experience.

item.title: dbreunig/nesformer
item.description: Drew Breunig has successfully embedded a functional Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) 6502 CPU emulator directly into the weights of a Qwen3.5-4B AI model. This project demonstrates the potential for using LLMs to emulate hardware, effectively allowing NES ROMs to run inside the neural network model.

item.title: Rejoice, leap seconds are dead!
item.description: The CGPM has officially decided to abolish leap seconds for Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), with the last one having occurred in 2016. This article explores the significance of this decision and provides context on the organization behind the change.

item.title: Elegance and intelligence are anticorrelated
item.description: This article explores the hypothesis that there is an inverse relationship between aesthetic elegance and analytical intelligence. It examines whether prioritizing simplicity and beauty in design or thought inherently limits complex problem-solving capabilities.

item.title: Making agents fast - what I've learnt over the last 12 months
item.description: This article explores practical strategies for optimizing AI agent performance, focusing on metrics like time-to-first-token and throughput. It covers technical approaches to tool integration, infrastructure design, and the necessity of robust sandboxing for efficient agent development.

item.title: Celebrating SIM Cards
item.description: The author reflects on the surprisingly seamless experience of swapping a SIM card into a new iPhone. Despite expecting typical technical hurdles, the process worked perfectly, leading the author to appreciate the success of standard mobile technology.

item.title: What I learned about power from LBJ and Robert Moses
item.description: The author reflects on the nature of political power by examining the lives of Lyndon B. Johnson and Robert Moses as chronicled by biographer Robert Caro. The piece serves as a preparation for an in-depth interview regarding the mechanisms and ethics of exercising influence.

item.title: Extremely brief history of PDP computers
item.description: This article provides a brief historical timeline of Digital Equipment Corporation's (DEC) PDP computer series. It examines the evolution, technical specifications, and market positioning of various models from the PDP-1 through the VAX transition.

item.title: A New Kind of Chemistry
item.description: This article explores innovations in chemistry through insights from Marathon Fusion. It highlights new chemical processes and potential advancements in material science.

item.title: Avoid Public Functions Calling Other Public Functions
item.description: This article advises against having public functions call each other to avoid unnecessary API coupling. It recommends refactoring shared logic into private helper functions to prevent public interfaces from becoming cluttered with internal implementation details.

item.title: Custom Voices With Qwen3-TTS
item.description: This post explores the author's experience using Qwen3-TTS to create unique, custom voiceovers for a dungeon crawler game project. It highlights the capabilities and limitations of Qwen3's three model variants, particularly regarding the trade-off between voice cloning quality and the ability to apply stylistic instructions.

item.title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
item.description: This piece explores the recurring frustrations of developers working with specific programming languages. It highlights the ironic persistence of preventable errors within language ecosystems.

item.title: API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions
item.description: OpenAI has introduced a new benefit where high-tier ChatGPT subscription plans now receive matching API credits. This move follows a similar recent announcement from Anthropic, providing users with increased flexibility to build and deploy AI projects.

item.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
item.description: Simon Willison explores Spawn, a multiplayer gaming environment where users utilize AI agents to generate and modify the world in real-time through prompts. The platform demonstrates the advanced potential of agentic engineering by allowing players to create structures and creatures like dragons within a voxel-based game.

item.title: Quoting Ben Hylak
item.description: This post highlights a humorous observation about the tension between the push for headless, AI-agent-integrated products and the enduring value of traditional user interfaces. It touches on the evolving role of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in the AI ecosystem.

item.title: You can just ask AI to do things
item.description: This article discusses the emerging paradigm of using AI systems as proactive agents that can execute tasks rather than just providing information. It emphasizes the shift from simple querying to delegating complex workflows to AI models.

item.title: Fake it ‘til you make it (and then keep faking it)
item.description: The article explores the psychological and professional implications of the 'fake it till you make it' mindset. It argues that maintaining this behavior beyond initial success is a functional strategy for sustained growth and overcoming imposter syndrome.

item.title: We Won’t “Just Hang Out”
item.description: This article explores the future of human connection in a post-Singularity world. It challenges the assumption that social interaction will remain unchanged or simply continue as casual 'hanging out' once human intelligence is fundamentally transformed.

item.title: This Week in Source Control: 28 October 2026
item.description: This blog post introduces a new weekly roundup dedicated to news in source control systems, clients, and forges. It highlights the inaugural edition, which features technical insights into Anthropic's transition from Git to their custom 'Scion' version control system to handle massive scaling demands.

item.title: The Unbalanced Group Theorem
item.description: This post discusses the classification of finite simple groups, recognized as one of the most extensive projects in mathematical history. It highlights the recent achievement by Axiom in formalizing the proof of the Unbalanced Group Theorem, a key component of this massive collective work.

item.title: C++/WinRT overcorrection: Using make_self and immediately converting it to the projected interface
item.description: This post critiques the practice of using 'make_self' in C++/WinRT when the result is immediately cast to the projected interface. The author suggests this approach is an unnecessary complication compared to standard instantiation methods.

item.title: Why don’t we run the taskbar and Task Manager at high priority, so they can remain responsive?
item.description: This post explains why assigning high priority to system components like the taskbar and Task Manager does not necessarily improve responsiveness. It highlights that system performance is often limited by dependencies and waiting for resources rather than just CPU scheduling.

item.title: Psychometrics, vaccines, meat, Kowloon, luggage destruction
item.description: This post reviews a scholarly paper evaluating the psychometric reliability of a 'Dynomight' version of the MBTI, showing high correlation with the original test. Additionally, it touches on the regulatory hurdles and bioethical controversies surrounding yeast-based vaccine self-experimentation.

item.title: Gadget Review: SoundPEATS CC3 Pro Bluetooth Headphones ★★★★⯪
item.description: This review evaluates the SoundPEATS CC3 Pro Bluetooth headphones, focusing on their unique 'clip-on' design. The author praises the device's exceptional comfort, noting that they can be worn all day without irritation.

item.title: Pluralistic: Agents vs ecommerce (28 Oct 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques the concept of 'agentic AI' in e-commerce, drawing parallels to his 2001 essay 'Metacrap' regarding the failures of the Semantic Web. He argues that the complexity of autonomous agents often clashes with the reality of proprietary web structures and conflicting incentives.

item.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
item.description: This post highlights insights from Ted Sanders on LLM performance and OpenAI's versioning strategy. It explains that while performance is multidimensional, model size remains the primary predictor of capabilities, and version numbers reflect release sequences rather than just incremental progress.

item.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
item.description: The 2026 GitHub Octoverse report highlights a massive surge in developer productivity, specifically noting that merged pull requests and commits have tripled. These record-breaking figures are attributed to the growing influence of agentic engineering and automated development tools.

item.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
item.description: The author identifies October 2026 as a major inflection point for 'vibe game development,' where advancements in AI models like Claude Opus 5.5 enable more sophisticated creation of 3D assets, music, and game design. By showcasing several successful experimental projects, the post argues that AI has evolved from producing superficial visuals to becoming a capable partner in actual game development.

item.title: Quoting Terk Terkowitz
item.description: Amazon's engineering leadership emphasizes that not every task benefits from AI, and identifying these limitations is a sign of good professional judgment. Engineers are encouraged to document where AI falls short and share these findings to help improve workflows.

item.title: Getting good at AI takes time and practice
item.description: The article emphasizes that mastery in the field of AI is not an overnight achievement but a result of consistent practice and sustained effort. It encourages readers to adopt a long-term mindset to navigate the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence.

item.title: I'm Full-Time Open Source Developer Now
item.description: Developer Miguel Grinberg shares his transition to working full-time on his 18 open-source projects. He explains the shift from balancing development with a day job and invites the community to support his ongoing efforts.

item.title: The upvote dilemma
item.description: Herman describes his decision to hide visible upvote counts on his platform, Bear, to reduce the 'popularity contest' dynamic and encourage content discovery based on merit rather than social proof. While keeping the underlying upvote mechanism for ranking, he aims to mitigate the negative psychological effects and the pressure to optimize for metrics.

item.title: Weekly Update 527: Cybergeddon News v. Reality
item.description: This update analyzes the recent hype surrounding 'Cybergeddon' headlines, noting that the predicted massive internet outages never materialized. It highlights the difficulty in verifying technical claims, specifically regarding the PHP2Shell exploit, contrasting sensationalist news with observable reality.

item.title: MTL-style circuit simulator
item.description: The article explores using the MTL-style pattern, a form of final tagless encoding, to build a circuit simulator in Haskell. It demonstrates how to define a clear boundary of operations through a type class to improve code structure and maintainability.

item.title: Inches & Miles
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: The article reflects on the history of internet startups harvesting user data through seemingly helpful features, such as Facebook's early 'Like' button. The author draws a parallel between this past era of digital exploitation and the current practices of AI startups, warning that history may be repeating itself.

item.title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False
item.description: This post discusses the Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) and the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which posits that no sub-exponential algorithm can solve 3-SAT. The author explores the implications of this hypothesis and recent theoretical developments regarding its validity.

item.title: Book Review: You Could Do Something Amazing with Your Life [You Are Raoul Moat] - Andrew Hankinson ★★★★☆
item.description: This blog post reviews Andrew Hankinson's book about Raoul Moat, praising its unique second-person narrative style. The reviewer highlights how the author avoids sensationalism by utilizing the subject's own words to provide a nuanced perspective on his life and actions.

item.title: Pluralistic: History is something you do (27 Oct 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow argues that the future is not a predetermined path but a contingent space shaped by human agency. He critiques the 'inevitabilism' promoted by tech influencers and policymakers, positioning science fiction as a tool to dismantle the idea that the future is beyond our control.

item.title: Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge
item.description: Simon Willison showcases a GitHub Universe conference badge that functions as a color computer capable of running NES and Game Boy Color emulators. Through collaboration, developers successfully ported classic titles like The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening to the badge's hardware.

item.title: Noctua Fan Swap on a Calnex Rb/GPS Frequency Reference
item.description: Jeff Geerling documents a hardware maintenance procedure for replacing a cooling fan in a Calnex Rb/GPS frequency reference unit. The guide covers the physical disassembly process, including dealing with Loctite-secured fasteners to access the internal components.

item.title: De IT-onmacht van de Nederlandse overheid
item.description: The author critiques the Dutch government's recurring struggles with information technology and their failure to acknowledge these systemic issues. Through two specific examples, the article argues that this denial prevents meaningful reform and long-term improvement.

item.title: Why My Dad Didn’t Have a Cell Phone
item.description: This post reflects on the increasing mental burden caused by modern communication tools that demand constant attention. It highlights the author's father, who foresaw this issue decades ago by rejecting cell phones to preserve his autonomy and personal time.

item.title: Package Management Devroom at FOSDEM 2027: Call for Participation
item.description: The Package Management devroom is returning to FOSDEM 2027 and is currently seeking talk submissions until December 1st. Organizers are looking for presentations from maintainers focusing on technical challenges like dependency resolution, supply chain security, and metadata standards.

item.title: Inversion in an ellipse
item.description: This post continues a series on geometric duality, focusing on the concepts of poles and polars in the context of ellipses. It explains the historical origins of these terms, tracing them back to spherical geometry and their subsequent extension to other geometric figures.

item.title: Where else to find me
item.description: The author outlines the various platforms where readers can find their work beyond the primary blog. This includes multiple specialized X accounts categorized by field and RSS feeds for updates.

item.title: Puzzling out why a program doesn’t work when run from a batch file, but works when double-clicked from Explorer
item.description: This post explains the technical discrepancies between executing a program via a batch file versus double-clicking it in Windows Explorer. It highlights how differences in environmental contexts and execution methods can lead to unexpected program behavior.
